1.note: Here, **my soul** represents Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I delight in him]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [behold **my chosen one**]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his **Spirit** were an object that he could place on Isaiah. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have empowered him with my Spirit]

Here, **the nations** represents the people who live in those nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [he will bring forth justice to the people who live in those nations]

2.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [He will not cry out; indeed, he will not lift up his voice]

Yahweh is using **lift up his voice** as a common expression of the culture to mean “speak loudly” or “shout.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will not raise his voice]

3.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of a weak, oppressed person as if that person were **a crushed reed**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a weak, oppressed person]

Here Yahweh is speaking of a weak, failing person as if that person were **a dim wick**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will not give up on a person who is about to fail]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **justice** and **faithfulness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [He will bring forth what is just and do it faithfully]

4.note: Here, the word **until** indicates the point in time up to which what Yahweh has just said about Isaiah remains true. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [this will continue to when he sets justice on the earth, and the coastlands will wait for his law]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [until he ensures that rulers govern fairly on the earth]

Here Yahweh is speaking of Isaiah as if he were a flame or a reed that could **become dim** or be crushed, as in the previous verse. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will not give up, and no one will stop {him}]

Isaiah is using the **coastlands** (the edge of the earth by the sea) to represent the whole **earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the whole world]

5.note: Isaiah is speaking of the **earth** as if it were a living thing that could give birth to offspring. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the earth and everything that grows from it]

6.note: The pronoun **you** refers to Isaiah, whom Yahweh is addressing. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I have called you, my servant,]

Yahweh is using **hold your hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “help and strengthen you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will help and strengthen you]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if Isaiah himself were **a covenant of the people**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will give you as the one who embodies my covenant with the people]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if Isaiah were **a light of the nations**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as one who guides the nations]

7.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of people who cannot perceive the truth as if they had **blind eyes** that Isaiah would open. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to help people understand the truth]

Here Yahweh is speaking of those whom Isaiah will rescue as if they were prisoners held in **the house of confinement**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the prison where they are confined]

Here Yahweh is speaking of those who are in captivity or ignorance as if they were **the dwellers of darkness**, people living in a dark place. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those living in captivity and ignorance]

8.note: Here, **my name** represents Yahweh himself and who he is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [that is my identity]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [nor will I give my praise to idols]

9.note: Yahweh is using the adjectives **The former** and **the new** as nouns to refer to certain kinds of things, namely former events and new events. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [The former things, behold, they have come, and the new things]

Yahweh is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

Here Yahweh is speaking of future events as if they were plants that **sprout** from the ground. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Before those new events come into being]

10.note: The word translated as **Sing** is an imperative, but it communicates a condition rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a condition for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a condition. Alternate translation: [May all sing to Yahweh a new song]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [sing his praise from the end of the earth]

Isaiah is referring to all the inhabitants of the world by naming two major components, those associated with **the sea** and those of **the coastlands**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everyone who lives in the world, whether on the sea or on the land]

11.note: Isaiah is speaking of **the wilderness and its cities** as if they were living things that could lift up their voices to sing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let the people who live in the wilderness and its cities lift up {their voices}]

Isaiah is using **lift up their voices** as a common expression of the culture to mean “sing aloud” or “shout.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let the wilderness and its cities shout aloud]
The word **Sela** is the name of a city.

Isaiah is using **the head of the mountains** to represent the highest part, or top, of the mountains. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the top of the mountains]

12.note: Here “them” refers to all the people. Alternate translation: [Let the people]

13.note: Here Isaiah begins speaking about Yahweh in the third person, and the pronoun **he** in the clauses that follow refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [This is what Yahweh will do: he will go forth as a warrior]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a warrior** is fierce and powerful in battle, so is **Yahweh** when he acts against his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will go forth, as fierce and powerful as a warrior in battle]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a man of battles** stirs himself up with zeal for the fight, so does Yahweh, who **will awaken zeal** against his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as a man of battles stirs himself up with zeal for the fight, so Yahweh will awaken zeal against his enemies]

Here Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh’s zeal as if it were someone asleep whom he could rouse, when he says that **he will awaken zeal**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will become very zealous]

The terms **shout** and **yell** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [He will shout loudly]

14.note: At this point Yahweh begins to speak directly. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to mark this explicitly.

The terms **kept quiet**, **been silent**, and **restrained myself** mean similar things. Yahweh is using these terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I have kept completely quiet from eternity]

The point of this comparison is that just as **one birthing** cries out loudly with pain and effort, so will Yahweh **cry out** when he finally acts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Like one birthing cries out loudly in pain and effort, I will cry out]

The terms **gasp** and **pant** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I will gasp deeply]

16.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the people’s lack of understanding as if they were **blind** people whom he would lead **by a way they have not known**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will make those who lack understanding walk by a way they have not known]

Yahweh is using the adjective **blind** as a noun to refer to a certain kind of person, namely people who are blind. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [And I will make the people who are blind walk]

16.q: בְּ⁠דֶ֨רֶךְ֙ לֹ֣א יָדָ֔עוּ בִּ⁠נְתִיב֥וֹת לֹֽא יָדְע֖וּ
16.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of how the people should live as if it were **a way they have not known** and **paths they have not known** along which he leads them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the way of right living that they have not known; on the paths of how to live rightly that they have not known]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the people’s distress as **darkness** and of his deliverance as **light**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will turn their distress into deliverance before them]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the difficulties the people face as **rough places** and of his removing them as making those places into **level ground**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the obstacles in their way into a smooth path]

The pronoun **them** refers to the people whom Yahweh has described as blind. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I will do these things, and I will not abandon those blind people]

17.note: The expression **They will be turned back** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [They will retreat]

The pronoun **They** refers to those who trust in idols, not to the blind people described in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Those who trust in idols will be turned back]

SPEAKER is repeating forms of the word **shame** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [they will be utterly shamed]
The phrase **the ones saying to a cast idol** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

18.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the people who do not respond to him as if they were **deaf ones** and **blind ones**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [O people who refuse to hear, hear, and O people who refuse to see, look]

19.q: מִ֤י עִוֵּר֙ כִּ֣י אִם־עַבְדִּ֔⁠י וְ⁠חֵרֵ֖שׁ כְּ⁠מַלְאָכִ֣⁠י אֶשְׁלָ֑ח מִ֤י עִוֵּר֙ כִּ⁠מְשֻׁלָּ֔ם וְ⁠עִוֵּ֖ר כְּ⁠עֶ֥בֶד יְהוָֽה
19.note: Yahweh has been speaking to the Israelites, but now he briefly addresses some other person or persons to speak about the Israelites. It is not clear who that person or those persons might be. However, the premise seems to be that the Israelites can still hear Yahweh as he speaks about them. Yahweh is doing this to express his feelings about the Israelites more powerfully. If a speaker of your language would not do this, you could translate these words as if Yahweh were speaking directly to Israelites about them. Alternate translation: [Who is blind except you, my servant, or deaf like you, my messenger whom I send? Who is blind like yoy, the covenanted one, or blind like you, the servant of Yahweh?]

19.q: מִ֤י עִוֵּר֙ כִּ֣י אִם עַבְדִּ֔⁠י וְ⁠חֵרֵ֖שׁ כְּ⁠מַלְאָכִ֣⁠י אֶשְׁלָ֑ח
19.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that his own servant is more blind and deaf than anyone else. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one is blind except my servant, and no one is deaf like my messenger whom I send]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his servant’s failure to perceive and obey as if the servant were **blind**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Who fails to perceive except my servant]

The expression **covenanted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the one with whom I have a covenant]

20.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the people’s failure to obey as if someone had **opened the ears** of a person who still did not **hear**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he has given them the ability to hear, but they do not listen]

Yahweh is once again speaking to some other person or persons about the Israelites, to whom he has been speaking directly. See how you translated the previous verse. Alternate translation: [you have opened your ears, but you do not hear]

21.q: יְהוָ֥ה חָפֵ֖ץ לְמַ֣עַן צִדְק֑⁠וֹ יַגְדִּ֥יל תּוֹרָ֖ה וְ⁠יַאְדִּֽיר
21.note: Here, the words **for the sake of his righteousness** mark Yahweh’s purpose that **he should magnify the law and glorify** it as the goal of his being pleased. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the sake of acting righteously]

22.note: The pronoun **it** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But the people of Israel are a people plundered]

The expression **plundered and looted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a people whom enemies have plundered and looted]

The terms **plundered** and **looted** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [a people completely robbed]

22.q: הָפֵ֤חַ בַּֽ⁠חוּרִים֙ כֻּלָּ֔⁠ם וּ⁠בְ⁠בָתֵּ֥י כְלָאִ֖ים הָחְבָּ֑אוּ
22.note: The expressions **trapped in pits** and **they are hidden** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [their enemies have trapped them all in pits and hidden them in houses of confinement]

Here Isaiah is speaking of the people’s captivity as if they were prey **trapped in pits**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all of them taken captive]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **confinement**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in houses where captives are kept they are hidden]
The phrase **none is saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

23.q: מִ֥י בָ⁠כֶ֖ם יַאֲזִ֣ין זֹ֑את יַקְשִׁ֥ב וְ⁠יִשְׁמַ֖ע לְ⁠אָחֽוֹר
23.note: Isaiah is using the question form to call the people to pay attention. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You among you who listen to this will attend and hear for afterward!]

The terms **attend** and **hear** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [will pay careful attention]

24.q: מִֽי נָתַ֨ן ל⁠משוסה יַעֲקֹ֛ב וְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֥ל לְ⁠בֹזְזִ֖ים
24.note: Isaiah is using the question form to lead his readers to acknowledge that it was Yahweh who handed Israel over to its enemies. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Jacob was given to the looter and Israel to the plunderers!]

Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that it was indeed Yahweh who did this. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It was indeed Yahweh]

The pronoun **him** refers back to Yahweh, the same person referred to by the word **whom** earlier in the sentence. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [against whom we sinned]

Here Isaiah shifts from the pronoun **we** to the pronoun **they**, but both refer to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [they sinned against him, and they were not willing] or [we sinned against him, and we were not willing]

Here Isaiah is speaking of obeying Yahweh as if it were **walking in his ways**, traveling along the roads that he marks out. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to live as he commanded]

25.note: The word translated as **So** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [Therefore he poured out]

Here Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh’s anger as if it were a liquid that he could **pour out** on the people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [So he unleashed his fierce anger on him]

The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, while the pronoun **him** refers to the people of Jacob and Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [So Yahweh poured out on Jacob and Israel]

Isaiah is using **the heat of his nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean intense anger. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his intense anger]

Here Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh’s anger as if it were a fire that **kindled** the people on every side. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it surrounded him on every side]

Here Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh’s anger as if it were a fire that **burned him up**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it completely destroyed Israel]

Isaiah is using **set to heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean to pay attention to something or take it seriously. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but he learned nothing from it] or [but he paid no attention]
